notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on Psalm 9, drawn from the sources accessible through your approved sites.

---

## Title and Superscription

**“For the choirmaster. To the tune of ‘The Death of the Son.’ A Psalm of David.”**

The Hebrew phrase is *al muth labben*. Most modern commentators regard this as the name of a tune to which the psalm was sung (Guzik, Enduring Word). The ancient Chaldee (Targum) paraphrase, however, renders it “Concerning the death of the Champion who went out between the camps,” referring to Goliath (1 Sam 17:4). The LXX and Vulgate read it as “concerning the mysteries of the son,” which led early Christian interpreters such as Augustine to apply the psalm to Christ, the only-begotten Son of God. Jerome understood the whole psalm as sung by the prophet in the person of the church concerning antichrist. The Syriac version titles it “concerning Christ, taking the throne and kingdom, and routing the enemy.” Others have suggested the death of Absalom or Nabal, though these fit less well. Still others take *labben* as referring to a Levite named Ben (1 Chron 15:18).

— Sources: Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-9/); StudyLight.org Cyclopedia entry on Muth-Labben (https://www.studylight.org/encyclopedias/eng/mse/m/muth-labben.html); Gill's Exposition (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-9.html); Ellicott's Commentary (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/9.htm)

**Psalms 9–10 as a single acrostic.** Ellicott notes that in the LXX and Vulgate, Psalms 9 and 10 are combined into one. This is likely the more ancient arrangement because (1) Psalm 10 is one of only two Davidic psalms in Book 1 lacking a title, suggesting it was originally joined to Psalm 9; (2) the combined piece is an alphabetical (acrostic) psalm, though imperfectly preserved. The Hebrew division was probably made later because Psalm 9 appears triumphant and Psalm 10 is a lament. Protestant Bibles follow the Hebrew reckoning.

— Source: Ellicott's Commentary (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/9.htm); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-9/)

---

## Verse-by-Verse Notes

**v. 1 — “I will give thanks to the LORD with all my heart; I will recount all Your wonders.”**

David opens with wholehearted thanksgiving. Spurgeon said, “Half heart is no heart.” The word translated “give thanks” (or “praise” in older versions) means to confess or declare openly; it is vocal praise with the heart fully engaged, not mere mental or half-hearted worship (Gill). “I will recount all Your marvellous works” refers especially to God’s redemptive miracles and unexpected deliverances, not necessarily supernatural miracles alone but any wondrous deeds of God in history and personal experience (Pulpit). Gill expands this to include creation, providence, redemption, the work of grace in regeneration, and future works such as Christ’s kingdom and the resurrection. David determined to make these the subject of his song.

— Sources: Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-9/); Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-9.html); Pulpit (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/9.htm)

**v. 2 — “I will be glad and rejoice in You; I will sing praise to Your name, O Most High.”**

David describes a second and third way of praising God: finding gladness in God himself, and singing praise to his name (character and nature). “Most High” (*Elyon*) was first used of God by Melchizedek (Gen 14:18–20) and was also a recognized divine name among the Phoenicians (Pulpit). The Chaldee paraphrase renders “I will be glad and rejoice” as “in thy Word” — i.e., the Logos, the essential Word of God (Gill). The two Hebrew verbs express great and even vehement joy.

— Sources: Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-9/); Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-9.html); Pulpit (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/9.htm)

**v. 3 — “When my enemies retreat, they stumble and perish before You.”**

Ellicott translates “in the turning of mine enemies back,” which may mean either “when they turned” or “because they turned.” The verb “fall” is better rendered “stumble” — through weakness, as the LXX has it. The enemy is portrayed poetically as thrown to the ground by the very glance of God’s fiery countenance (Hengstenberg, cited in Pulpit). Gill notes that this applies not only to David's physical enemies such as the Philistines when Goliath fell, but also to sin, Satan, the world, and ultimately antichrist — all of whom will retreat and perish at Christ's presence (cf. 2 Thess 2:8).

— Sources: Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/9.htm); Pulpit (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/9.htm); Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-9.html); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-9/)

**v. 4 — “For You have upheld my just cause; You sit on Your throne judging righteously.”**

David ascribes his victory entirely to God, not to his own skill or his soldiers’ valour. God’s favour was secured by the justice of David’s cause (Pulpit). While the battle raged, God sat on his heavenly throne administering justice — awarding defeat to the wrongdoers who had wantonly attacked his people, and victory to those standing in defence (Pulpit). Gill says God “maintained my right and my cause” by pleading and defending it, and by the flight and ruin of his enemies, making it clear that David’s cause was just. Guzik adds that this does not give believers licence to claim God is automatically on their side in every dispute; rather, it should make us endeavour to be on God’s side by conforming to his Word.

— Sources: Pulpit (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/9.htm); Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-9.html); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-9/)

**v. 5 — “You have rebuked the nations; You have destroyed the wicked; You have erased their name forever and ever.”**

The tenses in vv. 5–8 are “prophetic perfects” — describing coming events as if they have already happened, so certain is their fulfilment (Kidner, cited in Enduring Word). God’s rebuke is his punishment: when he punishes, he rebukes (Pulpit). To “blot out their name” means the family is extinct and its name erased from the civil register (Ellicott). Pulpit cautions that some allowance must be made for poetic hyperbole, since none of the nations David contended with suffered literal extermination. Gill interprets “the wicked” (singular in Hebrew) as pointing to Goliath, or Esau/Edom, or ultimately the man of sin — antichrist.

— Sources: Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-9/); Pulpit (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/9.htm); Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/9.htm); Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-9.html)

**v. 6 — “The enemy has come to eternal ruin, and You have uprooted their cities; the very memory of them has vanished.”**

Ellicott renders: “As for the enemy, they are made an utter wreck and perpetual ruin.” The KJV’s “O thou enemy” is a vocative that yields no clear meaning; the better translation addresses the enemy descriptively. The word “destructions” (*desolations, ruins*) comes from a root meaning “to be dried up.” “Their very memory is perished” points to the utter disappearance from history of once-great cities — perhaps Sodom and Gomorrah are in view as the archetypal example. Pulpit notes that this was fulfilled historically in the complete disappearance of the names Zoba, Beth-rehob, and Tob after David’s victory in 2 Samuel 10. The LXX and Vulgate read “with a sound,” referring to the crash of falling cities (Ellicott).

— Sources: Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/9.htm); Pulpit (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/9.htm)

**v. 7 — “But the LORD abides forever; He has established His throne for judgment.”**

The contrast is sharp: cities and nations perish, but Jehovah remains enthroned forever (Pulpit). Ellicott translates “Jehovah sits enthroned for ever,” in close parallelism with the next clause: “For judgment has erected his throne.” The Chaldee paraphrase reads “the Word of the Lord is for ever; his habitation is in the highest heavens,” applying it to Christ, the essential Word (Gill). The throne is established for judgment — not only temporal judgment in history, but also the final judgment after the resurrection of the dead.

— Sources: Pulpit (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/9.htm); Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/9.htm); Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-9.html)

**v. 8 — “He judges the world with justice; He governs the people with equity.”**

The “he” is emphatic — “he himself, and no other” (Pulpit). From his throne, God judges not only Israel’s enemies but the whole world, by a strict law of justice, rewarding all “after their deserving” (Pulpit). “In uprightness” is literally “in uprightnesses” — a Hebrew plural of perfection. Guzik notes that the Apostle Paul quoted this very line on Mars Hill: “He shall judge the world in righteousness” (Acts 17:31). Gill distinguishes between “the world” (the wicked) and “the people” (the people of God), to whom the righteous Judge will give the crown of righteousness.

— Sources: Pulpit (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/9.htm); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-9/); Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-9.html)

**v. 9 — “The LORD is a refuge for the oppressed, a stronghold in times of trouble.”**

The Hebrew *misgab*, translated “refuge,” is literally “a hill-fort” — a high, secure citadel into which the persecuted could retreat (Pulpit, Ellicott). Hengstenberg (cited in Pulpit) ascribes David’s use of this metaphor to his experience of safety in such places when fleeing from Saul (see 1 Sam 23:14). “Times of trouble” translates a rare Hebrew word (occurring only here and in Psalm 10:1) that Maclaren says means “a cutting off” — i.e., of hope of deliverance; distress intensified to despair (Enduring Word). The “oppressed” is literally “crushed” (Ellicott).

— Sources: Pulpit (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/9.htm); Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/9.htm); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-9/)

**v. 10 — “Those who know Your name trust in You, for You, O LORD, have not forsaken those who seek You.”**

To “know God’s name” is “to know him according to his historical manifestation; when one hears him named, to call to remembrance all that he has done. His name is the focus in which all the rays of his actions meet” (Hengstenberg, cited in Pulpit). Maclaren says it is “learning God’s character as made known by His acts” (Enduring Word). Those who know God in this experiential way place their trust in him because his track record shows he is thoroughly dependable. God has never in the past forsaken those who faithfully cling to him; they may feel forsaken (as in Psalm 22:1), but they are not actually forsaken (Pulpit). Trapp adds: “We never trust a man till we know him, and bad men are better known than trusted. Not so the Lord.”

— Sources: Pulpit (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/9.htm); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-9/); Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-9.html)

**v. 11 — “Sing praises to the LORD, who dwells in Zion; proclaim His deeds among the nations.”**

Having praised God himself (vv. 1–2), David now calls all faithful Israelites to join him (Pulpit). God “dwells in Zion” — enthroned on the mercy-seat between the cherubim in the tabernacle, now set up on Mount Zion (2 Sam 6:1–17). This limits the psalm’s date to after the ark’s transfer to Jerusalem. “Declare His deeds among the people” — in the original, “among the peoples” (plural), meaning not only Israel but all surrounding nations. David already holds the conviction that God’s revelation is ultimately for all nations (Pulpit). Spurgeon (cited in Enduring Word) remarks that “singing and preaching, as means of glorifying God, are here joined together,” noting that all revivals of gospel ministry — from Luther to Wesley and Whitefield — have been accompanied by outbursts of song.

— Sources: Pulpit (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/9.htm); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-9/)

**v. 12 — “For the Avenger of bloodshed remembers; He does not ignore the cry of the afflicted.”**

The expression “maketh inquisition for blood” (KJV) refers to God as the *Goel*, the Avenger of blood — the nearest relative of a murdered man who, according to Oriental custom, must avenge him (Ellicott; cf. Num 35:33–34). God is the ultimate Avenger who sees every murder and will require satisfaction. The blood of Abel spoke to God (Gen 4:10) and the blood of Naboth was seen by God (2 Kings 9:26). Spurgeon (cited in Enduring Word) applied this to persecuted believers: “O persecutors, there is a time a-coming, when God will make a strict enquiry after the blood of Hooper, Bradford, Latimer, Taylor, Ridley, etc.” The “humble” here is better translated “the afflicted” (Ellicott, following the Hebrew margin).

— Sources: Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/9.htm); Pulpit (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/9.htm); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-9/)

**v. 13 — “Be merciful to me, O LORD; see how my enemies afflict me! Lift me up from the gates of death.”**

After celebrating God’s care for the humble, David now prays that God would remember *him* in his own season of trouble. The shift from triumphant praise to personal plea has led some to see this as evidence that Psalms 9 and 10 were originally one psalm (Ellicott). “Gates of death” refers to Sheol — the realm of the dead — but Ellicott argues that “gates” here means “power” or “rule” (as in “Sublime Porte”), with the gate being the seat of the judge or king. There is a striking contrast between “the gates of death” and “the gates of the daughter of Zion” in the next verse (Spurgeon, cited in Enduring Word). The Pulpit Commentary takes “gates of death” more literally: David was habitually lifted up from the very brink of death.

— Sources: Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/9.htm); Pulpit (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/9.htm); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-9/)

**v. 14 — “that I may declare all Your praises — that within the gates of Daughter Zion I may rejoice in Your salvation.”**

David’s motive in asking for deliverance is not merely his own benefit but God’s greater glory — he wants to be rescued so that he can praise God all the more passionately (Enduring Word). “Daughter of Zion” is a personification of Jerusalem (cf. “daughter of Babylon,” “daughter of Edom”). Hengstenberg argues that “in the gates” means *within* the gates — i.e., in the temple, not amid the bustle of worldly business in the literal city gates (Pulpit). Spurgeon comments: “It is a good thing for the melancholy to become a Christian; it is an unfortunate thing for the Christian to become melancholy” (Enduring Word).

— Sources: Pulpit (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/9.htm); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-9/)

**v. 15 — “The nations have fallen into a pit of their making; their feet are caught in the net they have hidden.”**

The principle of poetic justice — the wicked fall into their own trap — is a recurring theme in Scripture (cf. Psalm 7:15–16). Whether David is looking back at a judgment already accomplished or forward in faith to one he confidently anticipates is uncertain (Pulpit). The metaphor of the pit and the net both express the same idea: God’s enemies are ensnared by their own stratagems. Guzik gives biblical examples: Haman’s gallows built for Mordecai, Joseph’s brothers’ plot, and Judas’s betrayal — in each case the evil plot served God’s purpose and destroyed the plotter.

— Sources: Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-9/); Pulpit (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/9.htm); Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/9.htm)

**v. 16 — “The LORD is known by the justice He brings; the wicked are ensnared by the work of their hands. Higgaion. Selah.”**

Ellicott translates: “Jehovah hath made himself known; He hath executed judgment, snaring the wicked in the work of his own hands.” God reveals his character — his justice, his refusal to acquit the wicked (Nahum 1:3) — precisely through the judgments he executes (Pulpit). The wicked are caught in their own devices.

**Higgaion. Selah.** This is the only place in the Psalms where these two terms appear together. *Higgaion* occurs three times in the Psalms: here, Psalm 19:14 (“meditation”), and Psalm 92:3 (Hebrew; “solemn sound”). Both meanings are etymologically possible. It likely indicates a musical direction — perhaps a pause for instrumental interlude, or a call for solemn meditation on the truth just stated. JFB says the combination “seems to denote a pause of unusual solemnity and emphasis.” Jamieson-Fausset-Brown adds: “In the view which is given here of the retribution on the wicked as an instance of God’s wise and holy ordering, we may well pause in adoring wonder and faith.” Clarke (cited in Enduring Word) paraphrases: “Meditate on this; mark it well.”

— Sources: Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/9.htm); Pulpit (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/9.htm); JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/psalms/9.htm); Cambridge Bible (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/psalms/9.htm); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-9/)

**v. 17 — “The wicked will return to Sheol — all the nations who forget God.”**

This is one of the verses where translations and traditions diverge significantly (see “Denominational and Translation Differences” below). The KJV reads “The wicked shall be turned into hell,” but Ellicott says this is “a most unfortunate rendering.” The Hebrew verb means “shall return” (LXX and Vulgate: *let them return*), not “be turned.” The destination is *Sheol* — the grave, the realm of the dead, the unseen world — to dust, according to the doom of Genesis 3:19 (Ellicott). The Pulpit Commentary agrees: “shall be turned backwards to Sheol, or Hades; i.e. shall be removed from earth to the place of departed spirits. There is no direct threat of retribution or punishment, beyond the *poena damni*, or loss of all that is pleasing and delightful in this life.” The Hebrew has an intensive double-direction form: “right down to the world of death” (Ellicott). “All the nations that forget God” is a poetic parallel describing the same group — the forgetters of God. Spurgeon remarks that “the forgetters of God are far more numerous than the profane or profligate,” and that “forgetfulness seems a small sin, but it brings eternal wrath upon the man who lives and dies in it” (Enduring Word).

— Sources: Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/9.htm); Pulpit (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/9.htm); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-9/)

**v. 18 — “For the needy will not always be forgotten; nor the hope of the oppressed forever dashed.”**

This verse forms a beautiful contrast with v. 17: the wicked forget God, but the needy are not forgotten *by* God (Enduring Word). The negative particle in Hebrew comes emphatically at the beginning, ruling both clauses (Ellicott). “Shall not always be forgotten” concedes that from the perception of the needy, they may for a time feel forgotten — but the good God promises this will not last forever. Clarke (cited in Enduring Word) says: “The needy, and the poor, whose expectation is from the Lord, are never forgotten, though sometimes their deliverance is delayed for the greater confusion of their enemies, the greater manifestation of God’s mercy, and the greater benefit to themselves.”

— Sources: Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-9/); Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/9.htm); Pulpit (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/9.htm)

**v. 19 — “Rise up, O LORD, do not let man prevail; let the nations be judged in Your presence.”**

David’s confidence in God’s ultimate judgment does not make him passive. Instead, he boldly prays, “Arise, O LORD” — a prayer for God to act now (Enduring Word). The Hebrew word for “man” here is *enosh*, which emphasizes frailty and weakness (Pulpit, Kidner in Enduring Word). That weak, mortal man should prevail over the eternal God is preposterous. “Let the nations be judged in Your sight” means: if they are judged, then, as being wicked, they are condemned; if condemned, then punished — defeated, ruined, brought to nought (Pulpit).

— Sources: Pulpit (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/9.htm); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-9/)

**v. 20 — “Lay terror upon them, O LORD; let the nations know they are but men. Selah.”**

The Hebrew phrase “put them in fear” (KJV) is literally “set fear to them.” The LXX, Vulgate, and Syriac read “place a lawgiver or master over them” — a different textual reading (Ellicott). With the present Hebrew reading, the sense is: “give such a proof of power as to trouble and subdue them” (Ellicott), either by striking panic terror into them or by causing them to see how dangerous it is to assail God’s people (Pulpit). The ultimate purpose is redemptive: “that the nations may know themselves to be but men” (*enosh* — frail mortals). G. Campbell Morgan (cited in Enduring Word) asks: “What prayer, then, can we pray which is of more vital importance than that the nations may know themselves to be but men? Such knowledge must drive them to dependence upon God, and such dependence is the secret of national strength.”

— Sources: Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/9.htm); Pulpit (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/9.htm); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-9/)

## Points Where Traditions Differ

### 1. The Unity of Psalms 9 and 10

The LXX (Septuagint) and Vulgate, followed by the Roman Catholic Church, count Psalms 9 and 10 as a single psalm. Protestant Bibles follow the Hebrew (Masoretic) reckoning which splits them. This affects the numbering of all psalms from Psalm 10 through Psalm 148. Internally, the combined psalm is an acrostic (alphabetical) poem, which supports original unity — but the acrostic is imperfect, with several Hebrew letters missing. Ellicott suggests a later writer may have adapted an earlier work and either disregarded or overlooked the alphabetical arrangement.

— Source: Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-9/); Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/9.htm)

### 2. The Title “Muth-Labben” — Tune, Event, or Christological?

- **Tune/Instrument view** (most modern Protestant scholars, including Guzik, Kidner): *al muth labben* is the name of a tune or musical instrument to which the psalm was sung.
- **Historical event view** (Chaldee Targum, some Jewish commentators, older Protestant writers): “Concerning the death of the Champion who went out between the camps” — i.e., Goliath. Others propose Nabal, Absalom, or an unknown Labben.
- **Christological/mystical view** (LXX, Vulgate, early Church Fathers, Syriac): “Concerning the mysteries of the Son” — applied to Christ’s incarnation, victory over death, or antichrist’s destruction. Augustine understood “the son” as the only-begotten Son of God. Roman Catholic tradition, following the Vulgate (*pro occultis filii*), has historically read the psalm through this lens.
- Spurgeon, while noting the uncertainty, preferred the “death of the son” reading because it “enables us to refer it mystically to the victory of the Son of God over the champion of evil.”

— Sources: StudyLight.org Cyclopedia on Muth-Labben (https://www.studylight.org/encyclopedias/eng/mse/m/muth-labben.html); Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-9.html); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-9/); Spurgeon's Treasury of David (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-9.html)

### 3. Verse 17: “Hell” or “Sheol” / “The Grave”?

- **KJV and some conservative Protestant traditions** (reflected in Guzik/Enduring Word, Spurgeon): “The wicked shall be turned into hell.” This is understood as a reference to eternal punishment in hell proper. Spurgeon speaks of “the nethermost hell” and “eternal wrath.” Trapp notes the Hebrew doubling “into hell” (twice), taken to mean “the lowest dungeon of hell.” This reading supports the traditional doctrine of eternal conscious punishment of the wicked.

- **Critical/modern scholarship and many newer Protestant translations** (reflected in Ellicott, Pulpit): The Hebrew is *lish'olah* — “to Sheol,” the realm of the dead, the grave. Ellicott calls the KJV “a most unfortunate rendering.” The Pulpit Commentary states there is “no direct threat of retribution or punishment, beyond the *poena damni* [loss of earthly life].” The NET Bible and most modern translations render it as “Sheol” or “the grave.”

This difference reflects a broader debate: does the Old Testament *Sheol* refer to the grave generally, or does it sometimes carry the connotation of the place of punishment for the wicked? The traditional Protestant devotional reading (Spurgeon, Guzik) tends to read the fuller New Testament doctrine of hell back into the psalm, while the critical commentaries urge a more restrained reading of what the original Hebrew would have conveyed to its first audience.

— Sources: Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/9.htm); Pulpit (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/9.htm); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-9/)

### 4. Gill’s Antichrist Interpretation

John Gill, the Baptist expositor, reads the entire psalm prophetically as concerning “the destruction of antichrist.” In his exposition, the “enemy” of v. 6 is antichrist (the Pope and the Romish system); the “cities” destroyed are the antichristian jurisdictions; “the wicked” of v. 5 is the “man of sin”; and the judgment described looks forward to the battle of Armageddon and the final establishment of Christ’s kingdom. This historicist reading was common among early Baptists and many Reformed Protestants, though it is less prevalent today.

— Source: Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-9.html)

### 5. The “Avenger of Blood” — God as Goel

Several traditions note that v. 12 portrays God as the *Goel* — the Kinsman-Redeemer who avenges blood. This has special resonance in Wesleyan and Holiness traditions that emphasize God’s care for the poor and oppressed, as well as in Reformed traditions that highlight God’s justice. The Pulpit Commentary and Ellicott both treat this as a straightforward reference to Genesis 9:5 and the ancient custom of blood-vengeance, now taken up by God himself. The same concept is developed differently in liberationist readings (not covered by the approved sources).

— Sources: Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/9.htm); Pulpit (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/9.htm); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-9/)

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship (Acrostic Structure and Dating)

The combined Psalms 9–10 form an alphabetical acrostic poem. The arrangement proceeds from *aleph* to *gimmel* (vv. 1–6), then *daleth* is missing. Four verses (8–11) begin with *vav*, then the arrangement proceeds to *yod* (v. 18). For *kaph*, *koph* is substituted (v. 20), and the acrostic picks up again with *lamed* in Psalm 10:1, where it soon breaks off. Ellicott concludes that “the authorship and date of the combined psalms cannot be ascertained. Their redaction for congregational use must be referred to post-exilic times.” This view — that the psalm in its final form is post-exilic — contrasts with the traditional ascription to David and the association with events from David’s life.

— Source: Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/9.htm)

### Catholic and Orthodox Readings

From the available search results, the key Catholic/Orthodox distinctive is the Vulgate and LXX reading of the title: *pro occultis filii* / ὑπὲρ τῶν κρυφίων τοῦ υἱοῦ — “concerning the mysteries (or hidden things) of the Son.” This led patristic commentators such as Augustine to read the entire psalm Christologically: “the Son” is Christ, and the psalm concerns his victory over death, his resurrection, his kingdom, and the judgment of the disobedient. Roman Catholic Bibles follow the LXX/Vulgate numbering, treating Psalms 9 and 10 as a single psalm (Psalm 9). The Syriac and Arabic versions likewise read the psalm as concerning Christ’s throne, kingdom, and victory over his enemies. No further distinctive Catholic or Orthodox commentary on individual verses was retrievable from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org within the search limits.
